title: Expert matching: Observable work may remain unsuitable
desc: Finds safeguards against insufficient service can outperform mere verifiability, while prices, trade and reputation remain unreliable quality proxies.

kps.k: Expert-service markets face a problem of matching work to need, not simply making work observable.
kps.d: The cluster frames legal services and other expert services as credence goods: customers may remain unable to judge whether work was necessary even after a successful outcome. It distinguishes insufficient service, unnecessarily costly service and billing for work not delivered. These failures require different safeguards. The legal-services connection is conceptual; the empirical evidence discussed chiefly concerns laboratory markets, healthcare, repairs and financial advice, not measured misconduct in legal services or AI deployment.

qs.q: The key feature of credence goods is that consumers do not know which quality of a good or service they need.
qs.a: On Doctors, Mechanics, and Computer Specialists: The Economics of Credence Goods · Academia · 2006

qs.q: The second problem mentioned earlier – putting a more expensive service on the bill than the one actually provided – is termed overcharging.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Pricing can align expert incentives in theory, but the efficiency result depends on restrictive conditions.
kps.d: Dulleck and Kerschbamer's benchmark predicts honest, efficient provision with homogeneous customers, commitment after diagnosis and either effective liability or verifiable delivery. Equal margins across treatments remove provision incentives under verifiability; uniform prices prevent overcharging under liability. This challenges the claim that information asymmetry alone necessarily causes fraud. However, the benchmark assumes observable costs, perfect diagnosis and honest treatment when experts are financially indifferent. Relaxing commitment, introducing heterogeneous customers with market power or hiding costs can restore inefficiency.

qs.a: On Doctors, Mechanics, and Computer Specialists: The Economics of Credence Goods · Academia · 2006

kps.k: Experimental evidence favours protection against insufficient service over documentation of delivered work, with enforcement qualifications.
kps.d: Dulleck, Kerschbamer and Sutter's 936-participant laboratory experiment varies liability, verifiability, reputation and competition. Liability strongly increases trade and efficiency, while verifiability has little effect, contrary to the standard prediction that either safeguard suffices. Liability rules out undertreatment in this design but does not reduce observed overtreatment or overcharging; verifiability prevents billing beyond delivery without establishing whether delivery meets need. The 2020 review treats liability as comparatively robust, while noting that failed service need not prove undertreatment, success may be unverifiable and extended liability can weaken customer care incentives.

qs.q: We study in a large experiment with 936 participants the determinants for efficiency in credence goods markets.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

qs.q: Summing up this subsection, it seems fair to say that, although verifiability and liability both yield full efficiency under the specific assumptions of DK06, liability outperforms verifiability in terms of robustness – in the sense that it increases efficiency under a broader set of alternative assumptions.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Lower prices, greater trade and stronger reputation do not reliably establish better treatment.
kps.d: The experiment finds that competition lowers prices and expands trade without generally reducing misconduct. Its conclusion identifies an efficiency exception under verifiability, whereas its abstract and the review frame the qualification around liability; these accounts should not become a single unconditional result. Reputation also shows limited, conditional effects: greater trust can increase transactions without reducing undertreatment. The review finds no systematic overall effect on fraud, while retaining exceptions involving trade, overcharging or diagnosis fees. Theory allows beneficial competition and reputation, but the evidence qualifies their ability to discipline hidden service choices.

qs.q: Competition among sellers has been found to be very influential in, first of all, bringing down the prices for credence goods (compared with a situation of a bilateral matching of sellers and consumers), and then increasing the frequency of trade on the market.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

qs.q: (2011), competition between sellers is found to have an impact on efficiency when combined with liability but not if liability is absent.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Expert motivations help explain departures from pure profit-maximising predictions, but do not supply a universal safeguard.
kps.d: Even under the experiment's least favourable conditions, sellers provide appropriate treatment in about half of cases. The authors interpret this as evidence that moral norms support exchange, and their heterogeneous-preferences model explains behaviour better in most conditions, though some pricing and overtreatment remain unexplained. The review adds that antisocial preferences can undermine equal-margin incentives and that apparently fair prices may signal expert type rather than cause honesty. Separate theoretical models predict that honest experts can increase trust that opportunistic experts exploit; this is not an empirical finding that honesty generally worsens markets.

qs.q: We start the conclusion by noting that even under the most disadvantageous market conditions for consumers the sellers of credence goods have provided an appropriate treatment in about half of the cases in our experiment.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

qs.q: Key to their argument are the following observations: First, the standard solution to the credence goods problem for markets with verifiability but without liability – equal-mark-up prices – is robust to the presence of sellers with pro-social other-regarding preferences, but non-robust to the presence of sellers with anti-social other-regarding concerns.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Diagnostic information is itself an incentive-design problem; more precision or disclosure need not always improve outcomes.
kps.d: The review reports laboratory evidence that diagnostic uncertainty increases fraudulent provision and reduces entry, lowering efficiency by about 16% in that setting. Liu and Ma's 2024 theoretical model addresses a different mechanism: privately observed continuous losses produce inefficient equilibria even when customers infer losses precisely, but allowing experts to choose a diagnostic information structure can restore first-best efficiency through a binary signal. These results do not directly contradict each other because the models differ. Liu and Ma provide no empirical evidence and assume risk neutrality, static information and contracts excluding partial repair. The review also finds that information revealing a serious problem can expose customers to more cheating when experts observe it.

qs.q: The experimental findings confirm the key predictions of the model: Diagnostic uncertainty not only increases fraudulent provision rates, but it also reduces market entry rates by consumers.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Practical remedies must preserve diagnostic incentives while targeting the specific abuse.
kps.d: The sources favour institution-specific analysis rather than a universal prescription. Separating diagnosis from provision can remove sales incentives, but collusion and lost economies of scope can offset the benefit. Second opinions improve correct treatment and efficiency in some experiments, while other models predict duplicated diagnosis, disruption of pooled pricing or failure to recover diagnostic costs. Insurance also changes provider incentives: a computer-repair field experiment reviewed by Balafoutas and Kerschbamer finds bills rise by more than 80% when providers learn that insurance will reimburse them, although insurance can still improve overall efficiency through increased service acceptance. For legal-service applications, the framework directs attention to enforceable obligations, billing observability, diagnosis funding and provider incentives; it does not establish that any particular pricing or technology reform will work.

qs.q: Intuitively, this could eliminate the incentives of experts to provide an inappropriate treatment recommendation, since they will not reap any financial benefits from selling the recommended treatment (unless they are able to collude with the agent who provides it).

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources accept the principal proposition and materially develop it through complementary theoretical, experimental and review evidence. Their common reasoning is that expert-service quality turns on whether provision matches an underlying need, which customers may be unable to assess even when delivered work is observable. They therefore distinguish safeguards against insufficient treatment from verifiability of delivery and caution that prices, trade and reputation are not dependable quality proxies. Material variation concerns mechanism and evidential status: the 936-participant laboratory experiment finds liability strongly improves trade and efficiency while verifiability has almost no effect; the literature review treats liability as comparatively robust but highlights enforcement limits and context-dependent effects; and the theoretical papers identify restrictive conditions under which pricing or deliberately designed diagnostic information can restore efficiency. Liu and Ma’s diagnostic-design result is theoretical and uses no data, while Dulleck and Kerschbamer’s pricing benchmark depends on assumptions such as homogeneous customers, commitment and effective liability or verifiability. Thus, these curated sources do not represent academia generally, but collectively strengthen the proposition while showing that no safeguard is universally effective.

qs.q: Liability to provide a sufficient treatment has been found to have a very strong effect not only on the likelihood of trade on our experimental credence goods markets, but also on its efficiency.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

qs.q: Contrary to our predictions, verifiability has been found to have almost no effect (compared to a situation where only moral norms may apply).
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources accept the principal proposition that observable delivery is not equivalent to suitable expert service and materially develop its institutional and incentive foundations. Both treat expert services as credence goods in which customers cannot independently match treatment to need, distinguish undertreatment from overtreatment and overcharging, and show why safeguards must target the specific failure. The theoretical source identifies restrictive conditions under which pricing plus either liability or verifiability can produce efficient service, while acknowledging that customer heterogeneity, market power, weak commitment and simplifying assumptions can restore inefficiency. The experimental source then sharpens the proposition empirically: liability against insufficient treatment strongly improves trade and efficiency, whereas verifiability alone has almost no effect; competition and reputation can increase transactions without reliably improving treatment. Material internal variation therefore concerns the potential of verifiability and pricing: the theory gives them a substantial role under idealised conditions, while the experiment finds verifiability much weaker in observed behaviour. This assessment applies only to the supplied curated sources and does not indicate the prevalence of these views among pre-2015 researchers.

elens.an: The 2020 review supports the proposition that observable delivery, lower prices, increased trade and reputation are unreliable indicators that an expert service was appropriately matched to the customer’s need. Its central distinction between undertreatment, overtreatment and overcharging explains why verifiability addresses billing beyond what was delivered but does not necessarily prevent unsuitable service. It also finds liability—protection against insufficient treatment—more robust across alternative assumptions than verifiability, while cautioning that liability can be difficult to enforce because failure does not prove undertreatment and success may not be verifiable. Material internal variation is institution- and context-specific rather than oppositional: benchmark theory permits efficient outcomes under restrictive assumptions; competition, reputation, disclosure and second opinions sometimes improve trade or efficiency, but can leave mistreatment unchanged or damage diagnostic incentives; and separating diagnosis from provision depends on collusion risks and economies of scope. The evidence base spans theory, laboratory experiments and field studies chiefly outside legal services, so it supports the general expert-market mechanism rather than establishing its incidence in legal services or AI deployment.

qs.q: Summing up this subsection, it seems fair to say that, although verifiability and liability both yield full efficiency under the specific assumptions of DK06, liability outperforms verifiability in terms of robustness – in the sense that it increases efficiency under a broader set of alternative assumptions.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

qs.q: Moreover, prices drop when sellers compete for buyers, but undertreatment does not decrease (and it even goes up from 53% to 73% when neither liability nor verifiability are in place).
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

elens.an: The supplied 2024 source builds on the cluster’s principal proposition. It accepts that legal and other expert services are credence goods in which customers may be unable to determine whether the service matched their actual need. Its material extension is to make diagnostic information itself an endogenous incentive-design variable: private expert knowledge can leave some needs untreated even when customers infer those needs precisely, while an expert-chosen binary diagnostic signal can achieve first-best efficiency. This strengthens the cluster’s warning that greater observability, disclosure or informational precision is not automatically beneficial. The contribution does not independently establish the cluster’s empirical conclusions about liability, verifiability, prices, competition or reputation. It is a theoretical model with no observational or experimental data, and its result is conditional on assumptions including risk neutrality, static information, nonverifiable treatment costs and the exclusion of partial repair. Thus, within this curated period evidence, it develops rather than merely repeats the proposition, while leaving the cluster’s institution-specific practical safeguards to other evidence.
